market_context: Stitchers who want to mount cross stitch on a rigid board for framing using lacing instead of adhesive on the fabric.
title: How to Lace Cross Stitch for Framing Without Adhesive

seo.title: How to Lace Cross Stitch for Framing Without Adhesive
seo.meta_description: How to lace cross stitch for framing by centering on board, temporarily securing, sewing opposite sides, adjusting tension and checking alignment.
seo.search_intent: Stitchers who want to mount cross stitch on a rigid board for framing using lacing instead of adhesive on the fabric.

excerpt: Lacing holds fabric to a rigid support with thread across the back. It can be adjusted and removed later without sticking the embroidery down.
content_html:
Lacing mounts cross stitch by wrapping the fabric around a rigid support and joining opposite margins with thread across the back. Instead of sticking the textile down, tension in the lacing keeps the piece centered and flat. It is useful when you want a mounting method that can be adjusted or removed later.

The goal is not drum-tight fabric. You are trying to remove waves, keep the grid straight and hold the textile evenly without distorting the stitches.

Prepare both stitching and mounting board first

Wash and press the piece when appropriate for the thread and fabric used. The embroidery should be completely dry and as flat as practical before mounting.

Cut a rigid board to the dimensions needed for the frame. When long-term preservation matters, choose framing material labeled acid-free or otherwise suitable for textile mounting.

Make sure enough fabric margin exists to wrap around the edges. When the cloth barely reaches the back, lacing becomes difficult and another mounting approach may be needed.

Center the design from the front

Place the board behind the fabric and measure visible space around the stitched design. Do not rely only on the cut edge of Aida because that edge may not be perfectly parallel with the weave.

Use fabric rows and equivalent points in the motif as references. Measure from the design to each board edge.

Small clean clips or appropriate temporary pins can hold the position while you turn the piece over to work on the reverse.

Lace the first pair of opposite sides

Fold the left and right fabric margins over the board. Using strong thread, stitch back and forth between those edges in long zigzag passes.

You are not sewing through the board. The needle passes only through the folded fabric margins and draws the two sides toward each other.

Create several passes before tightening fully. This spreads the load and lets you correct the centering without undoing the entire line.

Adjust tension gradually rather than pulling hard

After several laces, turn the mount over and inspect the front. If Aida lines begin to curve, reduce tension and redistribute it.

The textile should remain flat rather than stretched out of shape. Pulling strongly at one point can create a diagonal distortion or drag one corner inward.

Work progressively from the middle toward the ends. When the first axis is straight and secure, finish the thread without a bulky knot.

Repeat on the second pair of sides and flatten the corners

Fold top and bottom over the board and repeat the lacing perpendicular to the first set. Several fabric layers meet at the corners, so arrange them as flatly as possible.

Fold corners like a neat parcel so the bulk is distributed rather than concentrated directly behind one visible edge.

Check the front again. The motif should remain centered and the horizontal and vertical fabric lines should appear straight.

Inspect the mount inside the frame before closing it

Place the mounted piece into the frame temporarily and step back. Small alignment differences that were hard to notice on a table may become obvious once surrounded by a mat or frame edge.

If something is crooked, lacing can be loosened and adjusted without peeling the fabric from an adhesive surface.

Check depth as well. Folded textile, mounting board and any mat layers take more room than a normal photograph, so very shallow frames may not close comfortably.

Lacing takes more time than sticking fabric down, but it gives you control throughout the mounting process and keeps adhesive away from the embroidery. Work slowly, inspect the front repeatedly and aim for even rather than maximum tension. Once the design is straight and stable on the board, it is ready for the rest of the framing process.
